name: Portfolio Optimisation Beyond Mean and Variance
title: Portfolio Optimisation Beyond Mean and Variance
answer: Portfolio optimisation beyond mean and variance covers the methods used to choose asset weights when the classic trade-off between expected return and variance is judged too narrow. It takes in downside risk measures such as value at risk and expected shortfall, higher moments such as skewness and kurtosis, drawdown control, and constraints that reflect real mandates. In practice it sits between quantitative research and the portfolio manager's desk, where the output is a set of weights rather than a single forecast. The topic matters most where returns are not well behaved, which includes many concentrated or thinly traded markets.

sections.body: Portfolio optimisation beyond mean and variance covers the methods used to choose asset weights when the classic trade-off between expected return and variance is judged too narrow. It takes in downside risk measures such as value at risk and expected shortfall, higher moments such as skewness and kurtosis, drawdown control, and constraints that reflect real mandates. In practice it sits between quantitative research and the portfolio manager's desk, where the output is a set of weights rather than a single forecast. The topic matters most where returns are not well behaved, which includes many concentrated or thinly traded markets.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on price and return histories, factor exposures, and often a scenario or simulation engine that reprices a book under many paths. Data quality dominates: corporate actions, survivorship, and stale marks in less liquid names all distort the risk estimates that these methods depend on. Compute is usually modest by machine learning standards, since the bottleneck is often the optimiser and the number of resamples rather than the size of the model. Results are typically stored alongside the standard mean variance run so that the two can be compared on the same universe and date.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common route replaces variance with a coherent risk measure and solves the resulting problem numerically, since closed form answers rarely survive the added constraints. Where the objective is not convex, practitioners fall back on scenario based linear programming, convex approximations, or heuristic search. Estimation error is handled with shrinkage of expected returns, resampling, or robust formulations that assume the inputs are wrong within a stated range. Backtests are run with realistic turnover and transaction costs, because many of these methods buy their risk reduction by trading more. The result is judged on out of sample behaviour, not on the elegance of the objective.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Any deviation from mean variance has to be documented well enough for an investment committee, an allocator, or a regulator to follow the reasoning. That means recording the risk measure chosen, the constraints applied, the data vintages used, and the reason the standard approach was set aside. Model risk is the central concern, since a tail measure estimated from a short history can understate the very losses it is meant to capture. Where the strategy touches listed AI related instruments, the wider compliance picture matters too, and this site tracks 229 compliance and regulation pages alongside 150 active AI lawsuits as context for that exposure. Nothing here is investment, legal, or financial advice, and the material describes practice rather than recommending any position.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward risk measures that are easier to explain and to stress, and toward optimisation that treats the input estimates as uncertain rather than exact. Machine learning is entering mainly on the estimation side, for covariance and tail behaviour, while the optimisation itself remains largely classical. Expect more use of scenario libraries and climate or liquidity overlays as allocators ask for risks that a single covariance matrix cannot express. The open question is whether these methods generalise across regimes or merely fit the last crisis, and that is settled by live results rather than by backtest.
